name: Glassmorphism
era: 2007 (Windows Aero) - today; web wave 2020/21, platform renaissance from 2025
origin: The line starts with Windows Vista Aero (2007) and macOS Yosemite (2014), where window chrome first became translucent in order to show hierarchy without hard edges; Microsoft systematized this as Fluent Acrylic in 2017. Michal Malewicz coined the name 'glassmorphism' in late 2020, when backdrop-filter finally ran in every browser and the look exploded as a Dribbble trend. The biggest leap so far came from Apple with 'Liquid Glass', announced on June 9, 2025 at WWDC and shipped with iOS/iPadOS/macOS Tahoe/watchOS/tvOS/visionOS 26: instead of a static blur, Apple renders real-time refraction, specular highlights that react to device motion, and a coloring that takes its cue from the content behind. The style solves a real problem -- making layers visible without hiding the context underneath.
idea: Control surfaces are not paper but glass: they sit above the content, let it show through blurred and oversaturated, and mark their edge with nothing but a one-pixel refraction.
markers: backdrop-filter: blur(14-24px) saturate(160-180%) on every layer
Fill rgba(255,255,255,.08-.18) on a dark ground, .55-.70 on a light one
1px inner edge at the top (inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.4-.6)) as a light-catching edge
Radius 18-30px on panels, 999px on fields and floating bars
A busy ground is mandatory: gradient, photo or blurred color bodies -- on a flat surface the effect disappears entirely
At least two stacked glass layers (panel > row); depth comes from the stack, not from shadow
Drop shadow deep and wide: 0 18px 44px rgba(4,6,24,.45)
Apple's expanded version: lensing instead of blur, gyroscope-driven specular highlight, two material variants (regular / clear)
Text contrast varies measurably with the ground -- here 3.1:1 to around 16:1 within the same surface

params.radius: 18-30px on surfaces, 999px on pills, fields and action bars
params.contrast: low to medium, and above all: not constant
params.depth: Real layering: every layer blurs the one below; plus a wide, deep drop shadow and a light inner edge as a bevel
params.color: Color comes from the ground, not from the surface; the glass itself is colorless and merely oversaturates what shows through
params.type: Neutral, tightly set grotesque at 450-600, almost always white with a slight text shadow as a safeguard
params.motion: Soft and unhurried: 160-220ms cubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1) for hover and layer changes; on Apple additionally the traveling specular and the tab bar resizing on scroll
params.texture: Fine grain (10-18% opacity) against gradient banding; otherwise optically smooth

examples.name: Apple iOS 26 / macOS Tahoe 26 (Liquid Glass, 2025)
examples.what: Tab bars and sidebars that refract the content behind them instead of merely blurring it, with gloss edges that travel as the device tilts, and controls that shrink on scroll

examples.name: Microsoft Fluent Acrylic / Mica (Windows 11)
examples.what: Command bars and flyouts with a noise layer inside the material; Mica only picks up the wallpaper color without blurring live -- the performance-minded counter-proposal

examples.name: Apple visionOS
examples.what: The style in its most consistent form: windows really are panes of glass in space, casting shadows onto the actual surroundings

examples.name: Arc Browser / Dia (The Browser Company)
examples.what: Sidebar and command bar as glass surfaces over a colored space gradient -- the best-known web-native example

examples.name: Michal Malewicz, 'Glassmorphism in user interfaces' (hype4.academy, Dec. 2020)
examples.what: The text that set the term and codified the recipe (blur + transparency + 1px edge + colorful ground)

strengths: Shows layer hierarchy without hiding the context beneath -- neither flat nor neumorphism can do that
For overlays, modals, sticky navs and command palettes objectively the best available solution
Reads as high-end and current straight away, without a single graphic having to load
On Apple platforms from 2025 it is not merely allowed but the native system material -- free and correct there
Scales chromatically with the content: the same code looks different over every background image
risks: backdrop-filter is expensive: several stacked glass surfaces cause scroll jank on mobile and occasional repaint artifacts in WebView2/Tauri
Without a busy ground the style has no effect -- it forces gradients you may not want at all
Text contrast depends on whatever happens to be behind it; it cannot be guaranteed by token
The look visibly belongs to Apple right now: a web app of your own in Liquid Glass costume reads as a badly copied system app
Tips over into 'Bootstrap template 2021' as soon as the blur is too small, the transparency too high and the gradient too colorful
a11y: Contrast is a function of the ground, not of the design: white text in this demo sits between roughly 16:1 (over the dark base) and 3.1:1 (where a light color body stands behind the glass) depending on the spot -- so 4.5:1 per WCAG 2.2 AA is not met throughout, and secondary text drops locally to 2.4:1. That is why a dark tint of 34% sits beneath the white film here; without it the same text falls to 1.7:1. An opaque fallback under @media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) is mandatory as well -- Apple had to retrofit exactly that after the legibility criticism of macOS Tahoe, and to add a transparency slider to system settings -- and so is a style-breaking, opaque focus ring, because a 1px glass edge will never reach the 3:1 requirement of SC 1.4.11.
longevity: As a web trend the look is a distinct 2020s marker and ages middlingly; as a platform material on Apple devices it is set until the end of the decade at least. Using it on the web therefore means betting on someone else's platform brand -- and their next course correction (Apple has already lowered the default transparency once) hits your own product with it.

platforms.web: Technically available everywhere, but expensive and defensible only as a sparing decorative layer with an opaque fallback -- not as the base surface of the app.
platforms.mobile: On iOS from 26 the native and therefore correct route; on Android a foreign body, because Material 3 uses a completely different depth logic with tonal elevation.
platforms.desktop: Workable in Tauri, but WebView2 and WebKitGTK pay the GPU price differently; native window vibrancy via the Tauri effects API is the cleaner route than CSS blur.

verdict: As a brand basis: no -- as a component: yes, in exactly two places. The style is a platform material, not a trademark; make it the base surface and you look like a mediocre system copy on iOS and a foreign body on Android, and the recognition value belongs to Apple, not to you. For a solo developer it is also the only style in this family with real runtime cost, and it renders differently in Tauri depending on the WebView -- three platforms, three behaviors. It stays sensible where it solves a problem instead of setting a mood: command palette and modal overlay, each with an opaque fallback.
tip: Credibility comes not from the blur but from the edge and the tint. First: always set a light 1px inner edge at the top and a weaker one at the bottom (inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,.55)) -- without it glass looks like a milky film. Second: a dark tint of 25-35% belongs beneath the white film, because only that makes text contrast independent of the ground. And never drop saturate(180%): the oversaturation is what separates blur from glass.
